transcript.text: Samsung RS68A8820S9/EU flashing 22E on the display and the fridge side isn't as cold as it should be. What does 22E mean and can I fix it?

On Samsung fridge-freezers, code 22E typically indicates a fault with the evaporator fan in the freezer section. This fan circulates cold air from the freezer into the fridge; if it stops because of ice buildup or motor failure, the fridge side will go warm while the error flashes on the display. To fix this safely, I need to know if the freezer is still working. Is the freezer compartment still freezing properly (around -18°C), or is it warm as well? This tells us whether the compressor and cooling system are working correctly.

The freezer side is fine, it's still freezing properly and the ice maker and dispenser work. It's only the fridge side that's warm, about 9C with very weak airflow from the vents. No burning smell or tripping anything either.

Code 22E on Samsung fridge-freezers typically indicates a fault with the evaporator fan in the freezer section. This fan circulates cold air from the freezer into the fridge; if it stops because of ice buildup or motor failure, the fridge side will go warm while the error flashes on the display. Since your freezer is still freezing properly and there are no electrical tripping issues, the cooling system itself is likely working fine. The problem is probably that cold air isn't reaching the fridge compartment due to a blocked fan or duct. To confirm this safely: with the fridge door open, listen carefully near the back wall of the freezer compartment (where the cold air vents are). Do you hear a faint humming or whirring sound from that area when the compressor is running, or is it completely silent?
Not sure I can tell, to be honest. There's an occasional ticking/scraping sound from inside the fridge back panel, but I don't know if that's the same area you mean. Is that useful?

On Samsung models like yours, code 22E specifically points to an issue with the evaporator fan in the freezer compartment. This is the fan that pushes cold air from the freezer into the fridge section. This is not normal behaviour for a healthy appliance. To narrow this down safely: please unplug the fridge first. Once it's safe to touch, look at the back wall inside the freezer compartment (behind any shelves you can remove). Is there a thick block of ice covering that entire panel, or does it look relatively clear with only light frost? This will tell us if ice is blocking the fan or ducts.

Ok, I can unplug it. Just to check, the frost I can see is on the fridge side, a bit around the vent at the top back, not in the freezer. Do you still want me to look at the freezer back wall, and how long can I leave it unplugged? I've got a lot of food in there but I do have a cool box.

You can leave it unplugged for 24 hours; using your cool box with towels to protect the food is perfectly safe. Code 22E on Samsung models typically points to an evaporator fan issue or ice blocking the airflow. Since your freezer is still freezing properly, the compressor and gas system are likely fine. The frost you see in the fridge vent suggests that defrost water isn't draining correctly (or a heater has failed), causing ice to build up and block the cold air from reaching the fridge side. Please unplug the appliance now. Move your food into the cool box, remove any shelves or drawers that can be taken out easily, and leave both doors open for 24 hours to let all the ice melt completely. Place towels on the floor to catch water. Once it is bone dry, plug it back in and check if the cooling returns and the code clears.

Ok, I'll do the full defrost then. Just so you know, the frost is on the fridge side by the top back vent, not in the freezer. Should I leave both the fridge and freezer doors open for the 24 hours, and will the freezer food be ok in the cool box that long?

Yes, please leave both the fridge and freezer doors open for the full 24 hours; this ensures all internal ice melts completely. Your freezer food will be perfectly safe in a cool box for that duration, especially if you keep it tightly packed with towels or ice packs to maintain the cold. While you are doing this, I would also suggest checking the defrost drain hole at the bottom of the back wall inside the fridge compartment once it is dry; if it was blocked previously, clearing it now will help prevent the issue from returning quickly.
